articles.title: UK will miss climate targets if it weakens EV sales rules, advisers warn
articles.summary:
Analysts say mooted move to let more petrol and diesel vehicles be sold would wreck plan to reach net zero by 2050

Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the…
articles.byline: Jasper Jolly, Jillian Ambrose and Kiran Stacey

blocks.text: Weakening the UK’s electric car sales rules would probably cause the government to miss legally binding climate targets, according to advisers tracking Britain’s progress to net zero.

The analysis by the Climate Change Committee (CCC) suggests the policy would blow a hole in the plan for achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 – prompting concerns that Andy Burnham’s government will have to slash the UK’s carbon emissions reduction targets, known as the carbon budgets.
In a letter published on Wednesday, the CCC said the UK is “likely to miss” its climate targets if it confirms plans to allow more sales of petrol and diesel cars and vans in the next four years.
Those changes could result in an extra 8.4m tonnes of CO2 pollution a year from the UK by next decade.

The electric vehicle rules are the single biggest contributor to those climate goals, meaning the government will have to find other major carbon emission reductions, unless it amends the budgets to allow more pollution.
Carmakers must sell a bigger proportion of electric cars each year under the rules, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate, or face fines of £12,000 per vehicle.

However, the industry has lobbied intensively for months to cut the headline targets from 80% electric by 2030 to as low as 50% or 60%, arguing that the mandate was putting them under too much financial pressure.

Electric cars were 26.6% of UK new car sales during the first 10 months of 2026, well below the 33% headline target. However, carmakers are expected to comply with the mandate using a series of loopholes known as “flexibilities”.
The committee’s chair, Nigel Topping, wrote to Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, to oppose any reduction of the targets.

Such cuts would, he said, “put the government’s commitment to tackling climate change at risk, miss an opportunity to reduce costs for a typical household by about £800 a year, increase the UK’s exposure to volatile oil markets by up to 15m barrels of oil a year in 2030, and damage long-term competitiveness as our main export markets rapidly transition to electric vehicles”.
Some in government have become alarmed in recent months about the impact the government’s various changes could have on the UK’s ability to meet its climate commitments.

The government has just cut funding for installing heat pumps, the second-biggest decarbonisation policy. Burnham has also alienated some Labour MPs by waving through gas extraction from the Jackdaw gasfield, and considering approval for the massive Rosebank oilfield.
MPs voted earlier this year to approve a new set of carbon reductions for the years 2038-42.

However, the Guardian has learned that one cabinet minister in the Keir Starmer government wanted the government to go back to parliament to scrap those planned reductions and enact a more conservative target instead.
The idea did not come to fruition though, with other cabinet ministers mostly opposed.

An industry source with knowledge of discussions in government said that serious consideration was still being given to changing the carbon budgets in the run-up to the UN’s Cop31 climate conference, subject to parliamentary approval.
The source said it was not clear if the proposal was still being discussed. A government source strongly denied that it was under consideration.
The changes to the mandate also mean the UK is unlikely to meet the carbon budget covering 2033 to 2037.
after newsletter promotion

Several analysts said the government will struggle to find emissions reductions elsewhere, given the scale of pollution from petrol and diesel cars and vans. The policy could also face opposition from the governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, each of which have their own carbon budgets.
Burnham on Thursday told Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, that he was “proud to support this Cop’s focus on electrification” and urged people to choose electric cars and heat pumps.
Doug Parr, chief scientist at Greenpeace UK, said: “The Burnham government cannot talk of climate leadership on the international stage while doing a U-turn on ZEV targets at home.”

Topping added: “Weakening the zero-emission vehicle mandate would miss an opportunity to reduce the cost of living for people, undermine Britain’s competitiveness and leave us more exposed to volatile fossil fuel prices.
“People are buying electric vehicles in record numbers because they are cheaper to own than the alternative.
“The mandate gives those up and down the supply chain the certainty they need to invest, supports thousands of jobs, and keeps the UK on track to meet its climate commitments.
“British drivers deserve better than a backtrack on such critical policy.”

The car industry criticised the CCC’s analysis. Mike Hawes, chief executive of the Society for Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said: “A successful EV transition needs a strong market and a competitive industry.
“The CCC, however, ignores the damaging cost of the targets it defends: billions in unsustainable discounts and millions more in government incentives.
“Contrary to the CCC’s claims, the mandate is deterring local investment, as however much manufacturers export, without a strong local market there is no business case to build here.”

A government spokesperson said: “We remain committed to the phaseout of all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and to all new car and van sales being zero emission by 2035, as well as to our legally binding net zero targets.
“Our consultation on the mandate will not change this and will ensure we are taking a pragmatic and balanced approach to the ZEV transition.”

articles.title: Shabana Mahmood to launch fast-track training to improve police leadership
articles.summary:
After damning report into standards at the top of forces in England and Wales, 200 people a year with superintendent potential to be recruited

Hundreds of people will be trained to boost…
articles.byline: Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent

blocks.text: Hundreds of people will be trained to boost “frankly inadequate” leadership of law enforcement, the home secretary is to say.

Shabana Mahmood will tell police chiefs and leaders at their central London annual conference on Wednesday that standards must improve as she unveils a scheme to train 200 people a year, after a report in June into police leadership found it was at times “staggeringly” poor.

“The conclusions of the Police Leadership Commission were candid and eye-opening. Police leadership is inconsistent and, at times, it is frankly inadequate,” Mahmood will say, according to extracts released by her aides.
“This is the consequence of an earlier failure to invest in the development of future leaders.
“This government will address it … through the launch of a new fast-stream programme which will place hundreds of talented recruits on a path towards superintendent.”
Between 2023 and 2025, the police inspectorate graded two forces as inadequate, 13 as requiring improving and no forces as outstanding for leadership.
Also moving the home secretary to act was that eight serving or former chief constables were under investigation for misconduct across the 43 forces in England and Wales.
Mahmood will also mention that Devon and Cornwall was at one stage paying for three chief constables, with two of them at one point suspended.
The new scheme to recruit future police leaders will be open to people from any job and includes those who are not working in law enforcement.
The aim is to put recruits on a five to 10-year path to the rank of superintendent and “build a deeper and broader pipeline” of future leaders, according to government sources.
New future leaders will not need a degree and Mahmood’s advisers believe the scheme brings a “new focus and scale” to reversing the lack of emerging high-calibre police leaders.

Nick Herbert, co-chair of the leadership commission and a former Tory policing minister, said: “The introduction of a leadership fast stream is a significant step towards putting those recommendations into practice, and it is hugely encouraging to see this progress.

Lord Herbert added: “Effective leadership is fundamental to improving police performance, cutting crime and keeping the public safe. The challenges facing policing demand ambitious reform, and we must build on this momentum to deliver lasting improvements to leadership at every level of the service.”

Former Labour home secretary David Blunkett, co-chair of the Police Leadership Commission, said more changes were needed: “It is important that the introduction of fast-stream progression is not presented in isolation from the commission’s wider recommendations for a comprehensive overhaul of leadership competencies and career progression.

“Fast-track must not be seen as an elite mechanism, but rather as an opportunity, much like in the civil service, for those with the ambition and ability to accelerate their progression through the leadership and management ranks.”
after newsletter promotion

The Home Office said the 27 recommendations from the leadership commission are being considered. They include a new national academy of police leadership, and more money for leadership training, with a current spend of about £4m in a service costing £19bn a year.
The main question on chiefs’ minds is how many of the 43 police forces in England and Wales will be culled as part of the government’s planned radical changes.
Mahmood will not reveal how many big regional forces will be set up. The Guardian understands the still-unpublished review she ordered by Bernard Hogan-Howe recommended as few as nine.
But the home secretary’s speech will stress that local policing units will deal with everyday crimes if the changes go through, according to sources.
Police leaders have claimed a lack of money has put forces under strain.

Figures show that the early release of prisoners to ease overcrowding since March led to a 13% increase in arrests for breach of bail and an 8% increase in arrests so people can be returned to jail, compared with last year.
Police estimate this will cost forces £500m by March next year and fear the figure may rise.

articles.title: Brexit work travel rules need urgent improvement, say UK business leaders
articles.summary:
CBI says restrictions on cross-Channel work trips are hindering investment and trade between UK and Europe

Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to…

blocks.text: Business chiefs have called on the UK government and the European Commission to urgently ease Brexit restrictions on business travel for cross-Channel work trips.

A group representing industry bosses said it wants commitments from Andy Burnham and European political leaders that the restrictions will be one of the priorities in 2027 for furthering ties between the two sides, after a summit in Brussels this week.

The Confederation of British Industry (CBI), which represents some of Britain’s largest companies, welcomed the prime minister’s recent calls for a reset with Europe, designed to reverse some of the damage to Britain’s economy caused by Brexit.

But it said Brexit restrictions, which include making employees obtain work permits for travel, are deterring cross-border investors and hampering trade at the very time both sides are trying to build resilience against China.

Sean McGuire, the CBI’s director of Europe and international, said discussions should have been a priority in the talks this week, after a UK-EU summit in 2025 held by Keir Starmer also referenced improving business mobility.
“Very little has been achieved. In fact, practically nothing has been achieved. The emphasis was put on youth mobility,” said McGuire.

EU diplomats have said in the past that the UK pushed hard for improving business mobility but was met with resistance from the bloc, where member states see British services – a big export particularly in the financial sector – as a threat.
McGuire said that energy, defence and car industry bosses say they are being hampered by the inability to travel freely in Europe to service or run multinational operations.
He said the issue should be of interest to all sides as they build on multiple existing laws to protect European supply chains.

“Now that we’ve got youth mobility potentially in the Friday deal, we should move seriously to address the kind of business mobility, which would apply to both the goods sector and the services sector,” he said.
after newsletter promotion
British citizens travelling to the EU post-Brexit are restricted to 90 days at a time out of a maximum of 180 days a year, limiting companies’ ability to promote employees and travel.
“If you are a CEO of a multinational you can very quickly clock up 90 days,” McGuire said.

Separately, work permits have to be obtained for each country that a worker travels to. That can affect the servicing of equipment, particularly in engineering, where products that cost millions such as lifts, escalators and factory machines come with service and maintenance contracts.
“There is a big difference between irregular migration, which needs to be tackled, and business mobility, which is bringing investment into the UK and vice versa,” he said.
While an agreement is close on youth mobility, Burnham faces the same roadblock when it comes to opportunities for under-30s, who will be offered a three-year visa scheme to work, travel or study.
“It is a trick because the UK is negotiating with Brussels but work permits are a national competency,” said one EU diplomat.

But McGuire said there is a quick fix for business mobility, involving changes to the annex of the EU-UK trade and cooperation agreement, which allows the two sides to expand visa-free business travel across more industries without reworking the main treaty.

The CBI said it is also “disappointed” that no progress has been made on mutual recognition of qualifications allowing British or EU professionals to practise in each other’s territories as they did before Brexit.
Sources said there was a view in Brussels that mutual recognition of qualifications was more beneficial to the UK than to the EU, causing energy around the talks to drain away.

articles.title: Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat
articles.summary:
England’s exam regulator says those caught using AI or smart glasses face disqualification from GCSEs and A-levels

Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are…

blocks.text: Students in England could suffer “life-altering” penalties if they are caught relying on AI or smart glasses to cheat, England’s qualifications regulator has said.

The head of Ofqual, Ian Bauckham, said students could be disqualified from GCSEs, A-levels and other qualifications if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework, and called for retailers to be barred from marketing wearable technology for exam cheating.

“If you are caught committing malpractice with an important, high-stakes qualification … in extreme cases you can lose the entire qualification which, as I am sure you can imagine, can be life-altering for somebody’s future,” Bauckham told the Press Association.

As coursework submission deadlines near, Ofqual is launching a publicity campaign to make it clear to students that using AI for assessments such as extended essays and failing to declare it will not be tolerated.

Bauckham is also writing to examination boards in England to tell them that exam hall invigilators and supervisors should be trained to spot the “emerging risk” posed by wearable devices during next summer’s exam season.
He said he was increasingly concerned about the potential use of wearable devices during exams, especially those able to access AI.

In a speech to an education conference in Birmingham on Wednesday, Bauckham will say: “It is completely unacceptable for any retailer, online or otherwise, to market items explicitly for the purpose of exam cheating. This has to be challenged.”
Ofqual recorded 2,225 cases of smart device and mobile phone cheating during GCSE, AS and A-levels in the summer 2025 exam season.
Bauckham also suggested that the use of extended essays was under threat because of students’ increased access to AI.
after newsletter promotion
“We will need a radical rethink of the conditions under which it is done and the design of that coursework to make sure it is secure for the future and remains fit for purpose,” he said.
“Unsupervised extended essays, with no other forms of assessment associated with them … the time for that is likely to be quite short now.”
Academic subjects for GCSE and A-levels in England have had little or no coursework for the past decade, but A-level history and English are among those that still allow extended essays.

Bauckham said: “Where we do have extended writing being completed in unsupervised, uncontrolled conditions that is counting for coursework, counting for qualifications, I want … routes to malpractice, routes to cheating, to be closed down.”
Ofqual recorded 100 cases of plagiarism involving AI misuse in GCSE, AS and A-level entries last summer, an increase from 85 in 2024.
Bauckham said Ofqual was considering ways to guard against AI and plagiarism, including greater interrogation of the sources students use.

“It could mean linking the coursework in some formal way to the examination, whether that’s a written or a spoken examination, to make sure that we have a guarantee that students have genuinely done the work and genuinely understand it,” he said.

articles.title: Hugh Jackman, Rebel Wilson and 150 Australian artists join call to block Woodside gas development near Scott Reef
articles.summary: Actors, authors and musicians sign open letter urging Murray Watt to reject the fossil fuel company’s plan to drill for gas in Browse basin off Kimberley coast

blocks.text: More than 150 Australian artists, including Hugh Jackman, Rebel Wilson and Jessica Mauboy, have backed a Greenpeace-led campaign against Woodside Energy’s proposal to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast.

Woodside, the country’s largest fossil fuel company, describes Browse as “Australia’s biggest undeveloped offshore gas resource”. The oil and gas giant is hoping to win federal government approval to drill more than 50 gas wells about 3km from the Scott Reef area, which is home to more than 1,500 species, including endangered pygmy blue whales.

Actors Jackman, Wilson, Richard Roxburgh and Mia Wasikowska are among prominent Australians who oppose the Browse development on the basis that the proposed gasfield could damage the unique reef ecosystem.

They join musicians Jimmy Barnes, Paul Kelly, Tame Impala’s Kevin Parker, Tina Arena, Jessica Mauboy, G Flip, Vance Joy, Missy Higgins and Baker Boy in signing an open letter calling on the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, not to approve the development.

The letter – which says the Browse project “would turn Scott Reef into an industrial gas zone with decades of deafening seismic blasting [and] carbon dumping beneath the ocean floor” – was also signed by authors JM Coetzee, Helen Garner, Anna Funder and Diana Reid.

“Drilling at Scott Reef could cause an oil spill up to 30 times bigger than the 2009 Montara disaster, polluting Scott Reef with oil condensate, impacting the Kimberley coastline and even reaching as far as Indonesia,” it continued.

The open letter comes after a supergroup of more than 20 Australian artists – including King Gizzard & the Lizard Wizard, Barnes, John Butler and Montaigne – last Monday released If Not Now, a musical call to arms about the reef.
The song, a reimagining of King Gizzard’s 2020 track, If Not Now, Then When?, is a collaboration between Greenpeace Australia Pacific, Green Music Australia and p(doom) Records.
Browse, first proposed by Woodside in 2018, would see gas piped about 900km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant, which is adjacent to the world heritage-listed Murujuga rock art.

Last month, Guardian Australia revealed that WA’s independent environmental watchdog had sharply criticised the proposal, saying that plans to protect turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.
A draft letter from the Environmental Protection Authority, written in 2023, advised that it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level.
Greenpeace last month nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing, based on its ecological and scientific values.

Modelling by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis suggests that Browse would generate up to 6.8m tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions yearly at peak production, accounting for between 2.9% and 3.7% of Australia’s emissions in 2035.

“Browse gas is likely four times more expensive than existing domestic gas,” the institute found last year, adding that the project “is unlikely to be competitive either domestically or internationally, based on IEEFA cost estimates”.
Matt Roberts, executive director of the Conservation Council of Western Australia, earlier this month described Woodside’s proposal as “extremely concerning”.
“At the end of the day, we don’t need Browse gas. Western Australia has enough gas available to support us through the transition to a renewable future and regional demand for LNG is declining.
“The federal and state governments have enough evidence to reject this disastrous proposal and save Scott Reef, and we expect them to do just that.”

A spokesperson for the national EPA has told Guardian Australia the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.
A Woodside spokesperson said the proposed development “remains subject to a detailed, public and transparent assessment by state and Commonwealth regulators”.
Feedback had helped reduce “the infrastructure footprint around environmentally sensitive areas like Scott Reef – which will not be built on, drilled or mined”, they said.

“Browse is a natural gas and condensate development, not an oil development. References to a potential ‘oil spill’ from Browse are inaccurate.” The spokesperson added that the “longest credible duration of a potential well blowout, while still highly unlikely”, was around 12 hours.

articles.title: David Jones: what went wrong and what happens next? Five takeaways from first creditors meeting
articles.summary:
Upmarket retailer, which recorded a net loss of $228m last financial year, has total debt over $400m including $11m owed to staff

  • Get our

blocks.text: Upmarket retailer David Jones owed hundreds of millions of dollars when it collapsed into administration, after accelerating financial losses and reputational damage threatened its ability to stock shelves for Christmas.

About 500 creditors attended its first meeting on Tuesday, where administrators McGrathNicol started to break down who is owed what, when those left out of pocket will know where they stand, and what ultimately went wrong.
Here are five things we learned.
How much is owed?
David Jones collapsed early this month owing in excess of $400m to an assortment of creditors, including $180m of debts to trade creditors, mainly consisting of the brands that stocked its shelves.
There are also outstanding employee entitlements, such as annual and long service leave, worth about $11m, and about $33m in unredeemed gift cards, which the retailer is still accepting.

The rest is owed to large secured creditors, led by the retailer’s main financier, Hilco, which has a controlling hand over the current process and even has its own representatives in the 19 stores marked for closure.
Taken together, the debts are well over $400m, but that total is almost certain to climb as landlords tally up their losses.
On top of unpaid rent up to the appointment of administrators, shopping centre owners will also claim for broken leases after the chain’s receivers moved to close half of its 38-store network.
How much will creditors get back?

What, if any, money suppliers get back hinges on whether a buyer steps in and how much they are willing to pay, or whether the chain ends up liquidated, as well as how much cash David Jones can bring in through the crucial Christmas trading period.
Because product suppliers sit near the bottom of the creditor priority list, they won’t receive any money until secured lenders and employees are paid out.
Given the size of the outstanding debts, and poor financial state of the department chain, many suppliers are bracing for a near total loss of outstanding amounts.
Shaun Fraser, a founding partner at McGrathNicol, told creditors there were “too many variables” to indicate how much, if any, suppliers would receive.
“We haven’t yet got to a point where we’re engaged enough with bidders to have a sense of what value might be there,” Fraser said.
“We haven’t reached a point in the sale process where people are talking value or price.”
How are creditors feeling?
Store closures mean at least 1,689 jobs will go, plus those from brands with in-store concessions, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association (SDA) said Tuesday.

Bernie Smith, the SDA national vice president, said staff were stressed and did not know when they would be paid their entitlements. Only 170 staff were set to be redeployed, with offers to go out by Monday, he said.
Out of pocket suppliers are particularly frustrated, though the modern practice of holding meetings online kept any real anger contained behind muted microphones.
There were questions over whether there had been preferential treatment to some suppliers, and if the retailer had been trading insolvent before the appointment of administrators.
McGrathNicol said it would investigate when the company might have been insolvent, and if preferential payments were made.
after newsletter promotion
One brand representative said they had also repeatedly asked for stock lists and weekly sales figures without response.
What went wrong?
The administrators provided updated financials at the meeting that showed the poor state of affairs at David Jones.
The 188-year-old retailer recorded a net loss of $228m in 2025-26, before losing a further $69m in the first four months of the new financial year leading up to the administration.
Creditors were told that the funding pressures it was facing, coupled with reputational damage, was affecting its ability to get stock for the Christmas trading period.
David Jones ultimately got tipped into administration when negotiations with its main landlord, Westfield owner Scentre Group, broke down.

The retailer’s private equity owner, Anchorage Capital, wanted to radically reduce store numbers – something that is now happening during receivership – to rid the network of underperforming suburban stores.
The directors of David Jones listed several causes of the retailer’s problems, including everything from cost-of-living pressures and soft luxury demand to fierce online competition.
Fraser said there was also “clearly a business model problem” with the retailer.
What happens next?

Under a dual appointment, receivers FTI Consulting have taken day-to-day control of the business while administrators McGrathNicol hunt for a buyer, having called for “non-binding indicative offers” for the retailer by the end of the month.

That will trigger a process that could see formal bids lodged either late this year or early in 2027, giving some clarity to employees and suppliers ahead of the next creditors’ meeting, due by March.
The road ahead is, however, complicated by the breakdown in relations between Anchorage and the Westfield owner, which is threatening the retailer’s ability to operate at any of its complexes.

The Scentre Group chief executive, Elliott Rusanow, told Guardian Australia the landlord now had a “unique opportunity to facilitate the entry and growth of businesses that are more relevant to customers today and into the future”.
“That is the opportunity we will pursue at each of the 17 destinations with a David Jones store,” Rusanow said.

articles.title: 'A huge opportunity': Literary community ecstatic after P.E.I. author's Giller Prize win
articles.summary: After a Prince Edward Island author won Canada's most prestigious prize for literature, the province's literary community says it could mean more opportunities for writers here at home.

image.caption: Margaret Atwood, left, poses for a photo with P.E.I.'s Nicholas Herring after he won the 2026 Giller Prize on Monday. (CBC)

blocks.text: PEI·New
After a Prince Edward Island author won Canada's most prestigious prize for literature, the province's literary community says it could mean more opportunities for writers here at home.
Nicholas Herring took home $100K prize Monday for his novel Your Breath in Charcoal
Nicholas Herring won the $100,000 2026 Giller Prize, the top award for fiction in the country, for his second novel, Your Breath in Charcoal.
The author said he's relishing the opportunity the prize presents, and he's now figuring out his next steps.
"I just didn't think I was going to win so, yeah, I was quite shocked. I'm still quite shocked," Herring said.
"I got to twirl Margaret Atwood around on stage so, I mean, what do you say to that, right?... It's like a fever dream or something, you know? It's pretty awesome."
Island book lovers are big fans of 2026 Giller Prize winner Nicholas Herring
Aside from being an accomplished author, the native of Murray Harbour is also a carpenter and a fisherman.
Your Breath in Charcoal is his followup to 2022's Some Hellish, which won the Atwood Gibson Writers' Trust Fiction Prize.
Heather Doran, assistant manager at Bookmark in Charlottetown, said the business has been a longtime supporter of Herring's work.
She called Your Breath in Charcoal "a masterpiece" story about two Islanders who move to Toronto to work in the trades, and said Herring's Giller Prize win is "huge for writing on P.E.I."
"I think people forget that there's really good authors here because we're so small, and I think it's a great chance to put the Island writers on the map," Doran said.
"Last night in the ceremony, he said he had lots of books in him and we're greedy to always have a great book, so we can hardly wait to see what he does next."

Avid reader Bonnie Wonnacott was at Bookmark in Charlottetown on Tuesday picking up her copy of Your Breath in Charcoal, the Giller Prize-winning novel by P.E.I. author Nicholas Herring. (Barry Acton/CBC)
Bonnie Wonnacott was at Bookmark on Tuesday picking up the novel, which the avid reader said has been on her radar for a while.
After hearing the news of Herring's win Tuesday morning, she headed out to pick up her copy.
"When he decided to write this book, he said swing for the fences," Wonnacott said.
"I just thought what a beautiful metaphor for life … [and] just a reminder that ordinary people can do extraordinary things."

items: P.E.I. author Nicholas Herring wins 2026 Giller Prize for Your Breath in Charcoal
‘It doesn’t feel real’: P.E.I. writer Nicholas Herring reacts to Giller Prize longlist nod

blocks.text: P.E.I. Writers' Guild executive director Shawn Hogan said it can't be overstated how important Herring's win is to P.E.I. storytelling, and that having an Islander recognized on such a grand scale is a "massive achievement."

"He would do it regardless of accolades, regardless of that kind of recognition, so I think that more than anything is more inspiring to other writers that are just true writers at their heart, and that's what he is," Hogan said.
"I think it's going to have a tremendous impact that I don't even know if he would be aware of what it's going to do for Island storytelling for years to come."
LISTEN | Nicholas Herring on life after winning the Giller Prize — or at least the first 12 hours:
Mainstreet PEI9:06Nicholas Herring on life after winning the Giller Prize — or at least the first 12 hours
Since the win, Herring said his calendar has been getting pretty full with multiple talks and appearances planned.
He hopes to say something inspirational, and said he has a consistent message to impart: "You don't need permission to write a book."
"If you want to do it, go do it," Herring said.
"If I can write a book and win the Giller Prize, then you can, too. Like, it's that simple."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Lucas McInnis is a journalist at CBC Prince Edward Island. He can be reached at lucas.mcinnis@cbc.ca.
With files from Mainstreet P.E.I. and Tony Davis

articles.title: Nvidia reports bumper results as firm says it's not reinstating Huang
articles.summary: Nvidia reported strong quarterly earnings on Tuesday amid the dramatic exit of ex-CEO Jensen Huang.

blocks.text: "The board does not intend to reinstate him," Nvidia chair Harvey Jones said during a Tuesday call with financial analysts.

The company's profits also doubled from a year ago. For the quarter, which covered the three months to October 25, profit hit $65bn. Its revenue from data centres, a significant part of Nvidia's business, also doubled to $107bn in the same time period.
Going forward, the company said its rapid growth is poised to continue, and revenue will rise another 13% in the next quarter.
Given the uncertainty surrounding the company after Huang's exit, financial analysts had been unsure Nvidia would provide any forward-looking guidance.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior analyst for trading platform Capital.com, said Nvidia's results "offer a strong answer to concerns that demand for AI infrastructure is cooling" and temper immediate worry that Huang was irreplaceable as a leader.

"The harder question is whether Nvidia can preserve the strategic advantage Huang helped build," Hathorn added. "His exit is unlikely to change orders already committed, but could matter more when Nvidia makes its next round of decisions on products, partnerships and investment."
Kress seemed eager to stress that Nvidia can continue to not only succeed, but lead the ongoing AI buildout happening throughout the technology industry.
"It is business as usual," she said of what is happening inside of Nvidia now. "Our partners, our suppliers, all of them are 100% behind us."
She added that Nvidia's leadership team has "stood up very strongly over the last week... working seamlessly in all of their departments and projects".

"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed." Kress said before leaving the analyst call. "We've got this."

Despite board chairman Jones saying earlier that the company would not answer analyst questions about Huang or Nvidia's investigation into his conduct, he did address the search for a permanent replacement.
Jones said Nvidia is working with an executive search firm and is considering internal and external candidates, but that the company would not rush its selection.

"With the advanced technology and the national security dynamics in the marketplace, our new CEO will have to navigate those waters carefully," Jones said. "The search will be thorough and we want to do it as quickly as possible, but we won't do it before we find the exact right person."

articles.title: As Trump and Xi meet, China's AI dreams face an unexpected hurdle: the Nvidia spy scandal
articles.summary: China worries the scandal could ramp up pressure on the US to further restrict the sale of advanced chips.

blocks.text: Jensen Huang is out but his shadow looms over the upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping this week.

For Beijing, the former Nvidia CEO's dramatic fall is a major challenge - and not just because of claims that a Chinese spy may have honey-trapped Huang, one of the artificial intelligence industry's most influential figures.
Rather, the allegations surrounding Huang and his affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang are turning into a new flashpoint in an already fragile US-China relationship.
US intelligence reports claim she had ties to Beijing's intelligence apparatus - in particular the Ministry of State Security, China's main civilian spy agency.
The claim remains unproven, but it has already reignited debate in Washington over exports of advanced chips to China and whether the Trump administration has been too willing to ease restrictions.
For years now, advanced computer chips have been a key battleground in the US-China rivalry because they are essential for AI, supercomputing and military technology.
Chinese officials are worried this scandal could strengthen voices in Washington who argue in favour of further limiting Chinese access to cutting-edge American tech.

Just this week, the Trump administration introduced new export restrictions on Chinese firms that access advanced US chips in third countries such as Malaysia, Thailand or Brazil. They typically do this by renting computing power in data centres abroad to train their AI models. But some of the firms, like the one Alice Huang worked for, are also accused of smuggling chips to China, although they have denied this.

Until now, this controversy appeared to be a sideshow in US-China relations. But with Beijing calling the new rules "economic coercion" on the eve of Trump arriving in Shenzhen, there is a growing risk it could become something much bigger.

articles.title: No plans to reinstate CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia chair tells investors
articles.summary: Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened an investor conference call on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would ‌not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter.

image.caption: Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened an investor conference call on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would ‌not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter. (Dado Ruvic/Illustration/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New

Nvidia board chair Harvey Jones opened an investor conference call on Tuesday by saying the AI chip company would ‌not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions on the matter.
Huang had said he'd like to return to the tech giant after resigning over affair with Chinese businesswoman

Jones's start to a call about quarterly results was a forceful response to a movement to bring back Huang, who stepped down last week. With Huang gone, investors are eager for clues about Nvidia's future and strategy, from its commitments of billions of dollars to cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world's most valuable chipmaker.
Shares of the ​company rose two per cent in extended trading, after Nvidia forecast sales ahead of Wall Street targets.

"It's ​no surprise that they're doing very well, and there'll be people who will breathe a sigh of relief about it," said Rick Meckler, partner at Cherry Lane Investments. "But the story here is very complicated, and it's hard not to factor that in as an additional risk for ​people buying stock."

items: What the Jensen Huang scandal means for Trump and his administration

blocks.text: Jones said the board had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new CEO.

Interim CEO Colette Kress, ⁠who is also finance chief, kept her focus ⁠on financials and products in the statement accompanying results. "Our momentum is real," she said, without addressing ‌the leadership issue.
"Vera Rubin is off to an explosive start; our roadmap is on track," she added, referring to the company's latest flagship AI chip.
Lutnick faces scrutiny over Nvidia spy scandal
Huang suggested he'd like to return to Nvidia
Huang, the AI boom's most prolific salesman, resigned last Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang.

U.S. intelligence agencies are trying to determine the extent of Alice Huang's ties to China's Ministry of State Security and what information she may have passed ⁠to Beijing, according to two people familiar with the matter.
Jensen Huang's exit ended three decades of founder-led control over Nvidia's chip roadmap, customer deals and Washington ties, making execution a bigger risk than near-term AI ⁠demand, analysts say.

The company expects fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion US, plus or minus three per cent, above analysts' average estimate of $125.25 billion US, according to LSEG data. Nvidia said ‌the outlook assumes no data-centre chip sales to China.

items: U.S. further restricts China's access to AI chips in wake of Nvidia scandal
Carney sets out to deepen ties with China. Has the threat landscape changed?

blocks.text: Anshel Sag, principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Nvidia's outlook was "quite positive, albeit not as ambitious as in previous quarters, which many have already anticipated."

"I don't think anything near term will be affected by Jensen's departure," he said. "His executive leadership team is capable and has followed his leadership and executed effectively for years, reaching this point."

The board ​is considering internal and external candidates to replace Huang as CEO. But a growing "Stand With Jensen" campaign has complicated the search, and Huang said on Tuesday he would be "honoured" to return if the board ⁠deemed it best.
In this image taken from video provided by TVBS, Alice Huang attends a dinner hosted by Jensen Huang, in Taipei in May 2025. (TVBS/The Associated Press)
National security scrutiny

Earlier on Tuesday, Nvidia's board created a committee on national security and export controls, its first major governance move since ​Huang's departure, as scrutiny grows over the chipmaker's national security role.

Washington has also tightened licensing rules for chip shipments to ⁠Southeast Asia and overseas data centres serving Chinese firms, while lawmakers prepare to question Huang, ⁠who had pushed for greater chip exports to China.

Investors were already uneasy about AI ⁠spending ⁠after Democrats' midterm sweep fuelled fears of ​tougher scrutiny and slower data-centre expansion. They also want to know whether Nvidia's next CEO will continue ​financing customers, a practice that critics ⁠have called circular.

Tuesday's results offer a first read on Vera Rubin, Nvidia's newest generation of AI processors and successor to Grace Blackwell. Nvidia said in August that Vera Rubin would account for about a fifth of data-center revenue in the October quarter and forecast 70 per cent revenue growth in the ⁠next fiscal year.

articles.summary:
Students oppose appearance of self-described ‘race realist’ who made plagiarism claims against Jason Arday

Hundreds of protesters jammed the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford, to…

blocks.text: Hundreds of protesters jammed the cobbled streets around Oriel College, Oxford, to voice their opposition at an appearance by Nathan Cofnas, the self-described “race realist”.

The event organised by the university’s Reform UK student society – billed as “An evening with Nathan Cofnas: is DEI undermining higher education?” – went ahead on Tuesday evening despite opposition by students, college staff and local politicians concerned that his appearance would create a hostile environment.
Oriel, which allowed the Reform society to use a lecture theatre, declined to cancel the booking, saying it had a “statutory duty” to allow the blogger and academic to appear.
Earlier this year, Cofnas was the first to raise accusations of plagiarism against Prof Jason Arday.
Arday died weeks later, having resigned from his post as professor at the University of Cambridge, amid sustained media scrutiny which began with Cofnas’s claims.

The crowds outside sought to block the college’s main entrances, with hundreds chanting “Say his name – professor Jason Arday”, while several protesters held signs reading “Remember Professor Jason Arday”.

One of the protesters, a first year student studying English and German, who declined to give her name, said: “I think, given the situation at Cambridge with Jason Arday and given what happened, that we as an institution would be looking to not replicate that in any way or hinting that we could support that notion, [but] acting as an example in opposition.

“I think [Oxford and Cambridge], as two academic institutions, should be working together to banish this from ever happening again. And the fact that we can’t even act as the example, I think, makes me almost ashamed to be a part of this.”

blocks.caption: Nathan Cofnas was the first to raise accusations of plagiarism against Prof Jason Arday. Photograph: Adam Gerrard/Mirrorpix

blocks.text: Tommy, a second-year maths student at Oxford, said: “This is not the first of this kind of event. There was Tommy Robinson and the Oxford Union, and obviously there were protests for that as well. So I think it’s quite a nasty pattern that we’re seeing with these Oxford societies pandering to the far right, which is just really dangerous.”

Inside the lecture theatre, Cofnas was asked if he wanted to apologise to Arday’s family, but he declined. He said the implication behind the question was that “we shouldn’t criticise powerful figures”.
Cofnas added: “I would ask the people at Cambridge University who protected him for three years, who suppressed all criticism … I would ask them these questions,” earning a brief round of applause.

blocks.caption: A protester holds a sign condemning Nathan Cofnas over scientific racism. Photograph: Alicia Canter/The Guardian

blocks.text: About 40 people made it into the venue, with less than a third of the space filled. Protests outside could be heard throughout Cofnas’s talk. At times some members of the audience appeared disengaged, looking at their phone.
Cofnas spent the majority of an hour talking about the history of what he called the “race equality thesis”, and his reasons for questioning it.
He has previously written that black people would “disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment” under a meritocratic system.
Anneliese Dodds, the MP for Oxford East, said she had contacted Oriel College after receiving complaints from constituents.

Dodds said: “Cofnas’ views are both repellent and contrary to the facts. Many of my student constituents have therefore contacted me to express their concerns about the student reform society choosing to provide him with publicity.
“I have written to Oriel College to ask what they are doing to act on students’ concerns about this meeting, including on safety grounds.”

blocks.caption: An invitation from the Reform society for controversial academic Nathan Cofnas to speak at the University of Oxford's Oriel College hled to campus protests and a debate over free speech.  Photograph: Leon Neal/Getty Images

blocks.text: While the protests were largely peaceful, a group of police appeared towards the end of the event to clear protesters from the entrances.

Hannah, a first-year law student, said that the size of the protest was proof that “even if Oxford won’t listen to us and won’t cancel the event, we’re still going to show up and we’re going to show that we won’t let that decision silence us. And we will still show that we don’t approve of this and we don’t want this type of behaviour here.”
Misan Harriman, the photographer and former chair of trustees of the Southbank Centre, said he attended the protest because he was concerned by the “damaging” rhetoric that Cofnas espoused.
“The university has failed all the students, not just the black students, by having them see this as something that could be remotely seen as part of the course of free speech,” Harriman said.
Additional reporting by Stanley Smith and Beatrix Arnold.

articles.title: Thomas Markle charged over child sex abuse material in Philippines
articles.summary: Markle is being held in prison in the US on a separate charge and has previously denied all of the allegations.

blocks.text: Police in the Philippines have charged Thomas Markle Sr, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, with possession of and intent to distribute child sexual abuse material.
The charges were filed on Monday, Cebu province prosecutor Graeme Elmido told the BBC.

Earlier this month, the 82-year-old was separately arrested and charged in the US with possession of child sexual abuse material. The FBI said agents, after searching storage units Markle rented, seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books, that they allege contained child sex abuse material.
Markle, who is in custody, has previously denied the allegations. The BBC has contacted Markle's attorney in the US for comment.

Elmido told the BBC that Philippine National Police had charged Markle Sr with "two counts of intent to distribute CSAEM [child sexual abuse and exploitation material], and one count of possession of CSAEM material".
Last month, police in the Philippines obtained a warrant to examine devices allegedly removed from Markle's former home in the country.
Four boxes of material, including computers, phones, hard drives and old video tapes, were handed to officers by Meghan's half brother Thomas Markle Jr.

Earlier this month, Markle Sr was arrested and charged in the US. He had initially been placed under house detention at his assisted living facility in Florida, but was taken back into custody last week after prosecutors alleged he removed his ankle monitor.
Meghan Markle has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.
In a previously shared statement after the allegations against her father emerged, Meghan wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."
She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

articles.title: Israeli parliament elects new speaker backed by Netanyahu’s opponents
articles.summary:
Knesset’s appointment of Matan Kahana marks step towards reversing policies of outgoing government

The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back…

blocks.text: The Israeli parliament elected a new speaker on Tuesday, a key step toward rolling back policies passed by the outgoing government led by the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.
The new speaker is Matan Kahana, an ally of Gadi Eisenkot, the party leader currently working to form the next government and replace Netanyahu.
Eisenkot’s bloc has pledged to undo some of Netanyahu’s most contentious policies following Kahana’s election.

He was approved as speaker with 66 votes in the 120-member chamber, backed by the Jewish-led opposition parties and by the Arab-led parties. The candidate backed by Netanyahu’s bloc, Ofir Katz, received 52 votes following a stormy debate that stretched over seven hours.
“The appointment of Matan Kahana as Knesset speaker is a worthy democratic move that reflects the absolute majority in favour of change,” Eisenkot said ahead of the vote.

The vote took place weeks after the parliamentary elections on 27 October in which Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority. Eisenkot was subsequently tasked by Israel’s president with trying to form a new coalition government.
Eisenkot has up to five more weeks to secure enough alliances to form a coalition.
As negotiations continue on the sidelines, his bloc, along with unaffiliated Arab-led parties, can use their majority in the newly sworn-in Knesset to advance their legislative agenda.

They introduced several bills last week, including to set term limits on the role of prime minister, to form a government-led inquiry into the Hamas-led 7 October 2023 attacks and to reverse laws that limit the powers of the judiciary.
Kahana gives the opposition bloc a major legislative advantage, according to Assaf Shapira of the Israel Democracy Institute, a Jerusalem thinktank.
“It’s important because there is not much time, because the speaker of the Knesset can make the legislative process much, much faster or much slower,” Shapira said.
Kahana replaced Amir Ohana, a Netanyahu ally, as speaker.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot is tasked with trying to form a new Israeli government. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA

blocks.text: Eisenkot and his allies are under pressure to swiftly advance their legislative priorities in the weeks ahead. Roy Folkman, a member of Eisenkot’s Yashar party, heads the temporary committee that decides much of the Knesset’s work until a government is formed.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government, the Israeli president could give Netanyahu an opportunity to do so. That would probably give Netanyahu’s Likud party control of the committee.

Even though Netanyahu’s opponents would still hold a majority, they would “feel that their momentum has gone”, Shapira said, and there would be a “real danger that some of the legislation will be delayed”.

Chamber procedures will pose a further challenge. A bill has to be introduced on the floor, considered in committee and voted on several times on the floor before it passes the Knesset. That winding process could make it hard to move bills across the finish line before time runs out.

Shapira said Eisenkot and his allies are likely to prioritise rolling back controversial laws that gave the government a larger role in appointing judges and weakened the power of Israel’s attorney general, an independent role that is seen by many as central to Israel’s system of government checks and balances.
“It’s very easy to abolish these laws because no new institution has to be created,” he said.
Establishing a body to investigate the 7 October attacks would be easier, Shapira added, and carry greater legitimacy once a government is formed.
Netanyahu’s opponents argue he has blocked an independent probe into any military or intelligence failures around the day, the deadliest in Israel’s history, and evaded accountability.

articles.title: Oprah Winfrey names book by Ontario-born author as her latest book club pick
articles.summary: Previous Canadian books featured on Oprah’s Book Club include A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry and Fall on Your Knees by Ann-Marie Macdonald.

image.caption: Solace in Winter is a novel by Mary Lawson. ((Penguin Random House Canada, Richard Mobbs))

blocks.text: Books
Previous Canadian books featured on Oprah’s Book Club include A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry and Fall on Your Knees by Ann-Marie Macdonald.
· Hillel Italie
· Posted: Nov 17, 2026 5:28 PM EST | Last Updated: 27 minutes ago

Oprah Winfrey’s new book club pick is an acclaimed Canadian author’s novel about a small community in the late 1960s that’s upended by a young American who has crossed the border to flee the Vietnam War draft.
Solace in Winter, which Winfrey praised as "beautifully written and deeply moving” in a statement, is the November pick for Oprah’s Book Club.
“Solace in Winter reminds us that even in our loneliest moments, unexpected connections can open our hearts, heal old wounds, and change our lives in ways we never imagined,” Winfrey said.

Solace in Winter is a novel set in the small town of Solace in the winter of 1969. It follows a widower named Jack whose quiet life is upended when he finds a dog in a bad way and an injured American draft dodger on the road near his place.
He takes them both in, but when his daughter comes to visit one day, she makes a decision that she can’t take back.

items: 15 Canadian books coming out this November

blocks.text: “I was knocked sideways when Oprah phoned. In fact, to begin with, I didn’t believe it was her. I thought it was a hoax and I nearly hung up. But then she mentioned Solace in Winter, which at that stage hadn’t yet been published, and I thought, just a minute," Lawson told CBC Books in a statement.
"As a writer I am thrilled, of course. As a Canadian, at this particular time, I think it can only be a good thing that a Canadian voice will be heard on the other side of the border. ”

Lawson is also the author of the novels A Town Called Solace, Crow Lake, The Other Side of the Bridge and Road Ends. A Town Called Solace and The Other Side of the Bridge were longlisted for the Booker Prize.
Lawson, currently based in England, is originally from the small farming community of Blackwell, near Sarnia, Ont.

items: Mary Lawson's Booker Prize longlisted novel A Town Called Solace is a mystery about hope and redemption

blocks.text: Oprah's Book Club has been recommending titles since 1996 picked out by Winfrey herself. The book club began as a segment on the The Oprah Winfrey Show.

Previous Canadian books featured on Oprah’s Book Club include A Fine Balance by Rohinton Mistry, selected in November of 2001, and Fall on Your Knees by Ann-Marie Macdonald, selected in January of 2002.
